issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these items are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. 'Story Feels Unreal' and especially 'Overwhelm on Recall' imply a disjointed, emotionally intense trauma memory, which fits the strong Memory↔Threat links. In contrast, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests unusually easy narrative access to the trauma and directly pulls against the other memory items. For a severe PTSD profile centered on intrusive, overwhelming childhood domestic violence memories, this Memory combination is clinically inconsistent.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is incompatible with simultaneously being unable to put the event into words. This is a clear within-node inconsistency.

vignette: When Mara first fell into her father's kitchen at age nine, the sharp clang of a metal cup against wood was swallowed by the louder scream of her mother's voice, and the sight of her father's fists wrapped around her mother's wrists was seared into a dark, flickering memory that she could not put into words. The scene left her with a sense that she could not rely on herself to keep her safe, and that the people she loved could not be trusted. From that moment she began to doubt her own judgment, feeling as though she was forever in a state of unpreparedness. The thought that she might never be able to protect herself or trust others made the world feel like an ever-present threat, and she kept replaying the night in her mind, trying to find meaning where there was none. That internal voice of mistrust and self-doubt pushed Mara's perception of danger to the front of her awareness. Whenever she heard a sudden movement-a chair pulled out of a bar, a patron's abrupt shift in stance-she instantly felt a spike of alarm that told her something dangerous was looming. Each flash of the memory of her mother's cries, even when triggered by a mundane sound, amplified that alarm. The memory itself, when it surfaced, did not simply return; it brought with it a surge of feeling so intense that she could not continue speaking, and she would abruptly leave the conversation or shut her eyes. The memory's return only deepened her conviction that she could not rely on herself, and the conviction in turn intensified the sense that the world was hostile. In the dim lighting of the bar where she works, open spaces and sudden movements are routine. Mara has taken to rehearsing worst-case scenarios in her head before each shift, a mental rehearsal she believes prepares her for any potential threat. She checks that all doors are locked before closing, and she keeps a cautious distance from the crowd, staying close to the counter where the bar's layout feels less exposed. This ritual of checking and rehearsing not only heightens her perception of threat-she now feels more anxious in the presence of even harmless crowds-but it also forces the memory of that night to surface each time she rehearses. The more she rehearses, the more the memory invades her thoughts, and the more she feels that she cannot rely on her own judgment. Each time she locks a door, she confirms to herself that she is protecting herself from an unpredictable danger that will always be there. Mara's attempts to keep her emotions under tight control also tie her memories and threat perception together. When a memory swells up-when the image of her mother's eyes flash in the corner of her vision-she feels a rush of overwhelming emotion that she feels compelled to suppress. The act of trying to keep her feelings in check only reinforces the idea that she is unable to trust herself with her own emotions, further eroding her confidence. Her nightly routine of reviewing the event, then checking the house, then rehearsing the worst, forms a loop that becomes increasingly self-reinforcing. She has avoided the open balcony of the bar, which has made it hard to perform her job, and her colleagues have begun to ask if she wants to step away from the shift. She has stopped attending her usual social gatherings, fearing the open spaces that might trigger a sudden movement and a new wave of panic. Weeks turned into months. Mara's avoidance of open spaces grew into a full refusal to leave the bar's immediate vicinity during the day. She stopped going to the grocery store on the corner, preferring instead the corner shop inside the building where she felt a locked door at her back. The worst-case rehearsal became an everyday practice: before each shift, she mentally walked through the image of a violent confrontation, imagining the steps she would take to escape. Each rehearsal felt necessary, yet it only intensified her sense that she could not trust anyone or herself, and the memory of the abuse flooded each time she rehearsed, reinforcing the fear that she was in a perpetual state of danger. Now, after a week in which she could not bear the intensity of the memory and had to cancel a shift because the image of her mother's pain erupted so violently she could not keep her eyes open, Mara has decided to seek help. She has come to believe that her current routine is unsustainable, that her fear and her attempts to protect herself are only making her more isolated and anxious. The fear that pulling herself out of the bar and into therapy will bring the memories even more clearly to the surface lingers, but she also holds a fragile hope that if she can speak about what happened, if she can find a way to describe it in words, perhaps she can begin to change the pattern that has kept her in a cycle of threat, memory, and maladaptive strategies for over twenty years. She is afraid that she will feel the same panic in the first session, but she is also hoping to finally feel less terrified and more in control of her own life.
